(CNN) -- An Arkansas man suspected in a shooting that killed one soldier and wounded another at a Little Rock military recruiting center was angry over the treatment of Muslims, authorities said Tuesday. Pvt. William Long, 23, of Conway, Arkansas, was killed in Monday's attack. Abdulhakim Bledsoe, 23, of Little Rock, also told police he recently watched a video "pertaining to subversive activities which spurred him to commit this act," according to court documents. Bledsoe pleaded not guilty at his arraignment Tuesday and was ordered held without bail. He faces one count of capital murder and 16 counts of engaging in a terrorist act, said Little Rock Police Chief Stuart Thomas. The terrorist counts stem from the shots fired at an occupied building.  Watch scenes from Tuesday in court » . Before the not guilty plea, authorities said Bledsoe waived his Miranda rights after the shooting Monday and gave a video statement indicating that "political and religious" motives were involved. He "stated that he was a practicing Muslim ... that he was mad at the U.S. military because of what they had done to Muslims in the past," homicide detective Tommy Hudson said in a police report. Bledsoe told police "he fired several rounds at the soldiers with the intent of killing them," according to Hudson's report. The suspect is a Muslim convert who has also gone by the names Carlos Bledsoe and Abdulhakim Mujahid Muhammad. He changed his name from the latter April 23, citing religious reasons, court records show. A leader of the Muslim community in Little Rock said he did not know Bledsoe. The suspect had been under investigation after visiting Yemen, a federal law enforcement official said. The official declined to provide further information. Police believe the shooter acted alone "with the specific purpose of targeting military personnel," Thomas said. Kent Krause, Bledsoe's public defender, said a formal hearing would be held for his client, but no date has been set. Residents left flowers and miniature American flags outside the recruiting center after the shooting. A lone candle burned on the sidewalk next to bouquets of white and red roses. A note that said "Thank you for your service" was attached to the flowers. The shooting Monday killed Pvt. William Long, 23, of Conway, Arkansas, and wounded Pvt. Quinton Ezeagwula, 18, of Jacksonville, Arkansas, who were outside the military recruiting center. Bledsoe told police he was driving around and saw Long and Ezeagwula smoking outside the building, according to Hudson's report. He said he pulled into the parking lot and shot the two soldiers and added that "he would have killed more soldiers if they had been on the parking lot," according to the report. Ezeagwula was in stable condition Tuesday, the police chief said. The soldiers were part of a recruiting program called "hometown recruiting assistance," said Lt. Col. Thomas F. Artis, commander of the Oklahoma recruiting battalion that oversees the Little Rock Army-Navy recruiting center. Under the program, soldiers tell their stories to potential recruits. It's a volunteer position taken while soldiers are visiting or based back in their home region, Artis said. "I'm relieved there's a suspect in custody," said Capt. Matthew Feehan, commander of the recruiting center. He said several people were in the building at the time of the shooting, but nobody else was injured. Bledsoe was arrested after officers on Interstate 630 pulled over his car, which matched witnesses' description of a black Ford sport utility vehicle seen leaving the scene of the shooting. Police recovered three guns from the suspect's vehicle -- an SKS semi-automatic rifle, a .22-caliber rifle and a .380-caliber automatic pistol, Thomas said. The victims were shot with an SKS rifle, according to the police report. Police also seized from Bledsoe's vehicle and apartment several rounds of ammunition, two homemade silencers, handwritten notes in Arabic, CDs with handwritten Arabic labels, a computer and cell phones, according to court documents. Melvin Bledsoe of Memphis, Tennessee, was listed on the police report as Bledsoe's father. He declined to comment, referring questions to Little Rock police.

Before entering his not-guilty plea, Bledsoe waived his Miranda rights following Monday’s shooting and provided a video statement indicating that “political and religious” motives were involved, authorities said.

He “stated that he was a practicing Muslim ... that he was mad at the U.S. military because of what they had done to Muslims in the past,” homicide detective Tommy Hudson wrote in a police report.

According to Hudson’s report, Bledsoe told police that “he fired several rounds at the soldiers with the intent of killing them.”

The suspect is a Muslim convert who has also used the names Carlos Bledsoe and Abdulhakim Mujahid Muhammad. Court records show that he changed his name from the latter on April 23, citing religious reasons.

A leader of Little Rock’s Muslim community said he did not know Bledsoe.

A federal law enforcement official said the suspect had been under investigation after visiting Yemen. The official declined to provide additional information.

Police believe the shooter acted alone “with the specific purpose of targeting military personnel,” Thomas said.

Kent Krause, Bledsoe’s public defender, said a formal hearing would be held for his client, although no date has been set.

After the shooting, residents placed flowers and miniature American flags outside the recruiting center. A solitary candle burned on the sidewalk beside bouquets of white and red roses. A note attached to the flowers read, “Thank you for your service.”

Monday’s shooting killed Long and wounded Pvt. Quinton Ezeagwula, 18, of Jacksonville, Arkansas. The two soldiers had been standing outside the military recruiting center.

According to Hudson’s report, Bledsoe told police that he had been driving around when he saw Long and Ezeagwula smoking outside the building. (CNN) — Authorities said Tuesday that an Arkansas man accused of opening fire outside a military recruiting office in Little Rock—killing one soldier and injuring another—was motivated by anger over what he believed was the mistreatment of Muslims.

Pvt. William Long, 23, of Conway, Arkansas, died in Monday’s shooting. Pvt. Quinton Ezeagwula, 18, of Jacksonville, Arkansas, was wounded and remained in stable condition Tuesday, according to Little Rock Police Chief Stuart Thomas.

The suspect, 23-year-old Little Rock resident Abdulhakim Bledsoe, entered a not-guilty plea at his arraignment Tuesday. A judge ordered that he be detained without bail. Thomas said Bledsoe was charged with one count of capital murder and 16 counts of committing a terrorist act. The terrorism-related charges were based on gunfire directed at an occupied building.

Before pleading not guilty, Bledsoe had waived his Miranda rights following the shooting and recorded a statement suggesting that his reasons were both political and religious, investigators said. In a police report, homicide detective Tommy Hudson wrote that Bledsoe described himself as a practicing Muslim and said he resented the U.S. military because of its past actions toward Muslims.

According to court filings, Bledsoe also said he had recently viewed a video concerning “subversive activities” that prompted him to carry out the attack. Hudson’s report states that Bledsoe admitted firing multiple shots at the soldiers with the intention of killing them.

Bledsoe, a convert to Islam, has also used the names Carlos Bledsoe and Abdulhakim Mujahid Muhammad. Court records indicate that on April 23 he changed his name from Abdulhakim Mujahid Muhammad for religious reasons. A Muslim community leader in Little Rock said he was not acquainted with him.

A federal law enforcement official said Bledsoe had been investigated after traveling to Yemen, but the official would not disclose additional details.

Police believe he operated by himself and deliberately set out to attack members of the military, Thomas said. Bledsoe’s public defender, Kent Krause, said his client would receive a formal hearing, though a date had not yet been scheduled.

After the attack, local residents placed flowers and small American flags outside the recruiting office. Bouquets of red and white roses sat beside a single candle burning on the sidewalk, and a message attached to the flowers read, “Thank you for your service.”

Long and Ezeagwula had been standing outside the center when they were shot. Bledsoe told investigators that he had been driving nearby when he noticed the two soldiers smoking outside the building, Hudson reported. He allegedly said he entered the parking area and fired at them, adding that he would have shot additional soldiers if more had been present in the lot.

The two soldiers were participating in a program known as “hometown recruiting assistance,” according to Lt. Col. Thomas F. Artis, who commands the Oklahoma recruiting battalion responsible for the Little Rock Army-Navy recruiting center. Through the voluntary program, soldiers visiting or stationed in their home areas speak with prospective recruits about their experiences.

Capt. Matthew Feehan, the recruiting center’s commander, said he was relieved that a suspect had been apprehended. Several people were inside the office during the gunfire, he said, but no one else was hurt.

Officers arrested Bledsoe after stopping his vehicle on Interstate 630. The car matched witness accounts of a black Ford sport utility vehicle seen departing the shooting scene.

Thomas said investigators found three firearms inside the SUV: an SKS semiautomatic rifle, a .22-caliber rifle and a .380-caliber automatic handgun. The police report identified the SKS as the weapon used to shoot the two soldiers.

Court documents say investigators also confiscated ammunition, two homemade silencers, handwritten Arabic notes, compact discs bearing handwritten Arabic labels, a computer and several cell phones from Bledsoe’s vehicle and apartment.

The police report identified Melvin Bledsoe of Memphis, Tennessee, as the suspect’s father. He declined to discuss the case and directed inquiries to Little Rock police.

counterfactuals.output:
**Suspect targeted U.S. troops in deadly Little Rock recruiting-center attack, police say**

**LITTLE ROCK, Arkansas (CNN)** — A man accused of opening fire on two soldiers outside a military recruiting center Monday acted alone and was motivated by anger over U.S. military operations in Muslim countries, authorities said.

Pvt. William Long, 23, of Conway, Arkansas, was killed in the shooting. Pvt. Quinton Ezeagwula, 18, of Jacksonville, Arkansas, was wounded but survived. Both soldiers had recently completed basic training and were working temporarily with recruiters under the Army’s Hometown Recruiter Assistance Program.

Police said the soldiers were in uniform and standing outside the Army-Navy Career Center in west Little Rock on June 1, 2009, when a gunman fired at them from a vehicle.

The suspect, Abdulhakim Mujahid Muhammad, 23, formerly known as Carlos Bledsoe, was arrested a short time later. Investigators said weapons and ammunition were found in his vehicle.

Little Rock Police Chief Stuart Thomas said the attack appeared to have been “politically and religiously motivated” and that Muhammad specifically targeted military personnel. Police said Muhammad allegedly expressed anger over U.S. actions in Iraq and Afghanistan and the deaths of Muslims overseas.

Authorities said there was no immediate evidence that anyone else participated in the attack, though investigators examined Muhammad’s reported travel to Yemen and any possible extremist connections. Officials stopped short of saying the shooting had been directed by a foreign terrorist organization.

Muhammad was charged in state court with capital murder in Long’s death and attempted capital murder in the shooting of Ezeagwula, along with additional firearms-related counts. Prosecutors said the investigation remained active and that further charges were possible.

Long and Ezeagwula were not armed at the time, authorities said. Army officials described them as young soldiers beginning their military careers and said counselors and chaplains were made available to their families and fellow service members.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize everything known about the Little Rock recruiting center attack, including William Long’s death, Quinton Ezeagwula’s injuries, the suspect’s statements, and evidence recovered by police.
counterfactuals.output:
### Attack

On June 1, 2009, two U.S. Army soldiers were standing outside the Army–Navy Career Center on Rodney Parham Road in Little Rock, Arkansas, when a man in a black Ford Explorer Sport Trac drove past and opened fire with an SKS-style semiautomatic rifle. The soldiers were unarmed and participating in the Army’s Hometown Recruiter Assistance Program after completing basic training.

- **Pvt. William Andrew “Andy” Long**, 23, of Conway, Arkansas, was struck multiple times and died.
- **Pvt. Quinton I. Ezeagwula**, 18, of Jacksonville, Arkansas, was wounded, including a gunshot wound to the neck. He survived after hospitalization and treatment.

Investigators said the gunman fired roughly ten rounds. The recruiting office itself was not entered.

### Arrest and suspect

Police stopped the vehicle a short time later. The driver was **Abdulhakim Mujahid Muhammad**, born **Carlos Leon Bledsoe**, then 23. He was arrested without a prolonged confrontation.

Muhammad, an American citizen from Memphis who had converted to Islam, had previously spent time in Yemen studying Arabic and Islam. Yemeni authorities had detained him for immigration violations and deported him to the United States. His activities had attracted federal attention, but authorities had not developed evidence sufficient to prevent the shooting.

### Muhammad’s statements

According to police affidavits, interviews, letters, and later court proceedings, Muhammad:

- Admitted shooting the soldiers.
- Said he targeted them because they represented the U.S. military.
- Described the shooting as retaliation for U.S. military actions and the killing or mistreatment of Muslims in Iraq, Afghanistan, and elsewhere.
- Referred to the attack as **jihad** and said he acted “for the sake of Allah.”
- Said he would have killed more military personnel had more been present.
- Later claimed that the recruiting-center shooting was part of broader plans to attack military and, in some accounts, Jewish targets.

Muhammad also made claims suggesting ties to al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula or that he had been directed or encouraged while in Yemen. U.S. investigators, however, said they did **not establish that he was acting under the operational direction of a foreign terrorist organization**. He was generally treated as a self-directed or lone-actor extremist inspired by jihadist ideology.

In subsequent writings and interviews, he acknowledged that he was guilty under American law while arguing that he believed the attack was justified under his interpretation of Islamic law.

### Evidence recovered

Police recovered substantial physical evidence from Muhammad’s vehicle, including:

- The **SKS-type semiautomatic rifle** identified as the weapon used in the shooting.
- Additional firearms, reported as a **.22-caliber rifle and handguns**.
- Hundreds of rounds of ammunition—reports and court records commonly cite approximately **562 rounds**.
- Spent cartridge cases and other ballistic evidence connecting the rifle to the recruiting-center shooting.
- Materials indicating preparation for further violence, including military-related information and equipment. Searches connected to Muhammad also reportedly uncovered items such as homemade suppressor components and incendiary or bomb-making materials, though accounts differ on exactly where each item was recovered.

The rapid arrest, Muhammad’s admissions, eyewitness evidence, and the ballistic link between the recovered rifle and the shell casings left little dispute that he was the shooter.

### Prosecution and outcome

Arkansas prosecuted Muhammad for capital murder, attempted capital murder, and related firearms offenses. The case produced controversy over whether it should also have been handled federally as an act of terrorism. State and federal officials maintained that the state charges offered a direct and severe path to conviction, while critics argued that his ideological motive warranted federal terrorism charges.

In 2011, Muhammad pleaded guilty, avoiding a possible death sentence. He received **life imprisonment without parole for Long’s murder**, along with additional life sentences and other consecutive terms for the attempted murder of Ezeagwula and associated offenses.

The attack is widely regarded as a jihadist-inspired domestic terrorist shooting, although Muhammad was convicted under ordinary state murder and attempted-murder statutes rather than a federal terrorism statute.

**LITTLE ROCK, Ark. —** A Tennessee man accused of opening fire on two soldiers outside a military recruiting center told investigators he acted because of his anger over U.S. military operations in Muslim countries, authorities said, as federal agents examined his earlier stay and detention in Yemen.

Pvt. William Andrew “Andy” Long, 23, of Conway, Arkansas, was killed in the June 1, 2009, attack. Pvt. Quinton Ezeagwula, 18, of Jacksonville was wounded. Both had recently completed basic training and were working temporarily as Army recruiters when they stepped outside the Army-Navy Career Center in west Little Rock.

Police arrested Abdulhakim Mujahid Muhammad, 23, formerly known as Carlos Bledsoe, after a brief pursuit. Prosecutors charged him with capital murder and other offenses, describing the shooting as a deliberate attack on military personnel.

Little Rock Police Chief Stuart Thomas said Muhammad acknowledged firing the shots and indicated that his motive was both political and religious. According to investigators, Muhammad said he was angered by the deaths of Muslims at the hands of U.S. forces in Iraq and Afghanistan and had intended to kill soldiers. Authorities stressed that those statements were allegations to be tested in court and that the inquiry was continuing.

Investigators said Muhammad drove past the recruiting office in a dark sport-utility vehicle, turned around and returned before firing through an open window. The two soldiers apparently had little or no warning.

A witness in the area reported hearing a burst of gunfire and then seeing one uniformed man collapse near the entrance while another struggled after being hit. Other witnesses saw the SUV leave the parking lot and provided police with a description. Officers stopped Muhammad nearby after he was seen driving away from the scene.

Police said a search of the vehicle produced the rifle believed to have been used in the attack, along with additional firearms and ammunition. The seized items were reported to include an SKS-style semiautomatic rifle, a .22-caliber rifle, handguns, loaded magazines and homemade suppressor-type devices. Ballistics testing and forensic examination were ordered to determine which weapon fired the fatal shots.

Federal investigators also focused on Muhammad’s time in Yemen. He had converted to Islam and changed his name before traveling there, reportedly to study Arabic and Islamic teachings. Yemeni authorities detained him over immigration or visa violations and deported him to the United States in early 2009. The FBI had interviewed him after his return.

The bureau and members of a joint terrorism task force began reviewing his travel, contacts and activities in Yemen to determine whether he had encountered extremist figures or received training. Officials said publicly that they had not established that the Little Rock attack was directed by an overseas organization. The available evidence initially suggested that Muhammad acted alone, though investigators continued checking computers, telephone records and other possible connections.

Muhammad’s family said his behavior and beliefs had changed sharply after his conversion and foreign travel. His father later said the family feared he had been radicalized, but relatives also expressed shock at the accusation and sympathy for the soldiers’ families.

The shooting brought grief and heightened security to recruiting stations across Arkansas. Flowers, flags and handwritten messages accumulated outside the Little Rock office, while military personnel and local residents attended vigils for Long and offered support to Ezeagwula and his family.

Long was remembered in Conway as a friendly young man who wanted to serve his country. Ezeagwula was hospitalized and expected to recover.

Arkansas political leaders and military officials denounced the attack as a calculated assault on servicemen. Muslim community leaders in Little Rock also condemned the shooting, saying violence against innocent people violated Islamic teaching and warning that one suspect’s alleged ideology should not be attributed to the wider Muslim community.

Recruiters returned to work under increased police protection as the state murder case and the federal investigation continued.
